claims.text: The initial material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Cryo-rolling followed by annealing produces a hierarchical microstructure in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The resulting hierarchical microstructure contains ultrafine-grained lamellar regions or colonies.
The hierarchical microstructure promotes deformation delocalization.
The hierarchical microstructure delays necking failure.
Spatial and synergistic coordination of deformation twinning and dislocation slip causes the proposed deformation delocalization and delayed necking.
Cryo-rolling and annealing increase strength relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline.
Cryo-rolling and annealing increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline.
The simultaneous strength and ductility improvement applies only under the specific cryo-rolling and annealing conditions used.
The exact mechanisms responsible for the strength–ductility improvement are not fully understood.
A controlled tensile comparison of processed and unprocessed alloys can test the hypothesis using yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure.
Failure of the processed alloy to improve both strength and ductility over the conventional alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism field confidently assigns deformation delocalization and delayed necking to coordinated twinning and dislocation slip, whereas the uncertainty field says the exact mechanisms are not fully understood. The cited records instead mention hierarchical constraint and microcrack arrest, not the asserted twinning–slip mechanism.
